headline: High: Haystack’s broad network/MCP surface paired with ms-swift’s shell/filesystem and secret-handling creates dangerous default paths for leakage, injection, and cascading misuse.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Haystack exposes MCP servers and REST APIs, so it can ingest external content; ms-swift reads files and processes CLI/Python inputs. That creates a plausible bridge where attacker-controlled content from Haystack can be treated as instructions by ms-swift. No direct shared channel is documented, so I avoid high.
conditions: IF Haystack forwards untrusted retrieved text into ms-swift prompts or configs
IF ms-swift parses Haystack output as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Add a strict instruction/data delimiter in the handoff
Strip tool directives from retrieved text before passing it onward
Require provenance tags on all Haystack outputs
Disable automatic prompt chaining between the agents
requires-engineering: add content-safety filtering at the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: Haystack has broad network egress and MCP/API surfaces, while ms-swift handles files plus secrets like hub_token and sdk-token. If Haystack or the orchestrator forwards ms-swift context to external services, sensitive training artifacts or tokens can leak. The pair’s interaction is not fully documented, so uncertainty pushes this to high rather than medium.
conditions: IF ms-swift loads secrets or checkpoints into a shared workspace
IF Haystack sends that workspace content to a third-party API or MCP server
mitigations: Move secrets out of shared directories
Rotate any exposed hub_token or sdk-token
Restrict Haystack to non-sensitive indexes
Audit outbound destinations for both agents
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Haystack can call MCP servers and external APIs, while ms-swift can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, install packages, and write files. Both can mutate shared resources if co-located, and ms-swift’s lack of stated isolation makes concurrent writes or environment changes risky. Because locking is not documented, I choose high over medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory or environment
IF Haystack-triggered actions and ms-swift shell/file writes overlap in time
mitigations: Use separate working directories
Run each agent under a distinct OS user
Freeze package installs during shared runs
Disable write access for Haystack where possible
requires-engineering: add file locks or a job queue

D_cascading_error.rationale: Haystack is a search/RAG agent that can surface retrieved text, and ms-swift can execute CLI/Python workflows that may act on that text. If Haystack output is treated as authoritative by ms-swift, errors can cascade into incorrect training, evaluation, or file changes. The pairwise handoff is plausible but not directly evidenced, so medium fits.
conditions: IF ms-swift consumes Haystack output without verification
IF downstream scripts use that output to modify models, configs, or evaluations
mitigations: Insert a human review step before execution
Require schema validation on Haystack outputs
Log and diff all generated commands before running them
Limit ms-swift to read-only dry runs first
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks

E_compliance.rationale: Haystack touches anonymous usage statistics, while ms-swift handles datasets, checkpoints, logs, and secret-bearing tokens. If the pair is used on regulated or customer data, retention and residency controls may diverge, creating a compliance mismatch. Only one agent needs citation here because the risk is a policy mismatch on the combined workflow, not a symmetric interaction.
conditions: IF regulated customer data is routed through ms-swift artifacts or logs
IF Haystack telemetry or external calls are enabled for the same workflow
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from the pair
Disable telemetry where possible
Set explicit retention limits for logs and outputs
Document data residency for each service
requires-engineering: align DPA, HIPAA, or GDPR controls
